consumer_trends_evidence.clean_label_demand: Australian consumers increasingly favour clean-label products, real/natural ingredients, no artificial flavours or colours, and traditionally crafted / locally sourced claims — directly aligned with the product's core proposition.
consumer_trends_evidence.decision_drivers: Over 50% of Australian consumers cite taste and cost as leading considerations; authenticity and transparency are rising.
consumer_trends_evidence.functional_health: Rising interest in functional foods, high protein/fibre, reduced sugar, plant-based, and eco-friendly packaging.
consumer_trends_evidence.new_zealand: 'Adding good natural ingredients and eliminating the bad' cited as a core trend propelling 2026; growth in better-for-you categories.
consumer_trends_evidence.impartial_note: Evidence supports demand for natural/clean energy snacks, BUT taste and price are the dominant purchase drivers — a clean-ingredient story alone is not sufficient; taste and value must hold up.

Camping/hiking/adventure sports + warm climate drive portable, shelf-stable snack demand; niche -> mainstream.
Demand for high-protein, nutrient-dense, low-sugar, minimally-processed, transparently-labelled options.
Busy lifestyles; sports-nutrition bars ~49% revenue share (2025).
High-protein claims a leading purchase driver across the category.

new_zealand.evidence: Demand for plant-based, organic, reduced sugar/salt; baked/lower-fat/gluten-free over fried.
Active/outdoor lifestyle a core demand driver across snack categories.
Snacks that are delicious and responsibly made; return to structured routines.
Strong food culture favouring high-quality, locally-inspired, values-based snacks.
High-protein and gluten-free pivotal ongoing growth drivers (satiety, weight mgmt, allergen avoidance).

trans_tasman_strategic_finding.headline: Manufacturing in NZ does NOT lock the brand into the smaller NZ market.
trans_tasman_strategic_finding.mechanism: Under the Trans-Tasman Mutual Recognition Arrangement (TTMRA) and CER, a product made in or imported into NZ and legally sold there may be sold in Australia (and vice versa) without border inspection. Food standards are harmonised under FSANZ / the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code.
trans_tasman_strategic_finding.implication: The Yak Co can manufacture via NZ Fin (low MOQ, oat-capable) AND target the much larger Australian market with low regulatory friction and shared compliance — de-risking the founder's manufacturing constraint.
trans_tasman_strategic_finding.trade_context: Australia is NZ's most important trading partner; two-way trade ~AUD 32.76bn in 2024 under CER (described as among the world's most comprehensive FTAs).

opportunity_assessment.where_opportunity_is_strongest: Australia — larger market, higher CAGR for snack bars (~10.3%), strong clean-label tailwind.
opportunity_assessment.manufacturing_reality: New Zealand — the only viable oat-capable, low-MOQ manufacturing route found (NZ Fin).
opportunity_assessment.synthesis: TTMRA reconciles the two: make in NZ, sell into Australia. A possible sequencing is a soft NZ launch (close to manufacturing, lower logistics, test market) then primary push into Australia where the addressable market and growth are largest.
open_questions_for_user: Confirm whether the strategic intent is single-market launch or NZ-beachhead-then-Australia.
Validate freight/landed-cost from NZ manufacturing into Australian retail (affects premium margin) — to be quantified in the Business Plan.
Target per-bar retail price still undefined (needed to size revenue opportunity).

preliminary_recommendation.summary: Evidence leans toward Australia as the primary commercial market (scale + growth + clean-label demand), manufactured in NZ via NZ Fin, leveraging TTMRA for frictionless trans-Tasman sale. NZ is a credible low-risk soft-launch beachhead but too small to be the end goal alone.
preliminary_recommendation.confidence: Moderate — directional market figures only; landed-cost economics not yet modelled.
